title_original: T3 Photo in Tokyo: Fruitful Liaisons
excerpt_original: The area just west of Tokyo Station, lined with tall office and retail towers, carries a history its facades barely hint at. “This is where the city’s first photo studios were born, where Utagawa Hiroshige (the master of Japanese woodblock prints, editor’s note) spent the last…

blocks.text: The area just west of Tokyo Station, lined with tall office and retail towers, carries a history its facades barely hint at. “This is where the city’s first photo studios were born, where Utagawa Hiroshige (the master of Japanese woodblock prints, editor’s note) spent the last years of his life; it is also where kabuki theater flourished in the Edo period,” Ihiro Hayami, director and founder of the T3 urban photography festival, enthusiastically recounts. To reach skyscraper lobbies, building gables, or a café-gallery, he takes the neighborhood’s historic backstreets rather than its broad avenues. On these walls and facades, 18 artists from Japan and abroad are on view for 24 days, free of charge.

Reconnecting with the history of the place, to “forge an identity and bring life to it,” in the words of T3’s creator: the event’s commitment echoes this year’s minimal, inspired theme, “と” (to), meaning “and.” “It is a coordinating conjunction that sets things against each other but also brings them together,” Ihiro Hayami explains. “We wanted to reflect on the duality this word implies, as another way of thinking about the world, modeled on the Asian philosophy of yin and yang.”

blocks.text: Zanele Muholi’s large-format self-portraits take over the vast glass hall of the Midtown Yaesu complex. There is no escaping this gaze, which forces a face-to-face encounter, eye to eye. In the exhibition “When Things Become a Crown,” Zanele Muholi, a leading figure of visual activism in South Africa, blends opposites by staging these carefully dressed reflections of the self. Clothespins and safety pins, paper rolls and rubber gloves were the tools of alienation of Muholi’s mother, a domestic worker employed by a white family under apartheid. Muholi wears them to reclaim their history, their origins, their identity, and to denounce the discrimination experienced by Black communities past and present, down to the way they are represented, a convention the artist plays with. Pushed to extreme contrast, these monochrome images celebrate Muholi’s Africanness and the color of their skin, long poorly rendered by film stock calibrated for white skin, and the target of racist practices such as the “pencil test”: a pencil pushed into the hair was used to assign racial classifications under apartheid, which the artist’s headdress of combs subtly evokes.

blocks.text: A short distance away, on the walls of a café-gallery in the neighboring Kyobashi district, the exhibition “Trace and Vision” showcases the work of Japanese photographer Sayaka Uehara. A recipient of the prize awarded by the town of Higashikawa, on the island of Hokkaido, home to an international photography festival every summer, the artist sheds light on the darker side of her native archipelago, Okinawa, held captive by the idealized images that cling to it: paradise beaches and lush landscapes. “To reflect on the problems facing Okinawa (…), I had to go beyond simply observing its landscapes,” the artist says. Far from these postcard views, her images capture a seemingly ordinary daily life: a backyard, a wrinkled hand, a waiting room where time seems to have stood still.

Each of Sayaka Uehara’s images forms a complex mosaic, studded with rough edges, that maps Okinawa’s many layers. “I believe photography has the power to make visible things that are accessible to everyone, yet neglected, ignored, or forgotten,” the artist continues. The wounds of the colonial past (once the Ryukyu Kingdom, the archipelago was annexed by Japan in 1879), economic inequality, and the overbearing presence of American military bases surface in a scene, a detail: a worn building, Coca-Cola red parasols planted in the sand, a barbershop for soldiers, a Kerama deer crossing an empty street. “When I take the time to look at my photographs, I feel that every element in them bears witness to something, a small voice that cannot quite be put into words,” she says.

blocks.text: Shifting the gaze. Nozomi Suzuki’s photographs, the second half of this duo exhibition, question our anthropocentrism by drawing attention to the images objects create on their own, “without human intervention or intention,” the artist specifies. The vent in a saucepan lid, a hole nibbled by an insect in a leaf, a tiny cavity in a piece of wood: every opening in our surroundings becomes a chance for the photographer to slip in her device inspired by the camera obscura. Using a lensless wooden camera, she turns these everyday apertures into a way of capturing images and watching the world exist in our absence. “These images usually go unnoticed, blending into the ambient light, but even when we pay no attention, light is constantly creating images,” Nozomi Suzuki tells Blind . “I feel that these invisible images are like monologues whispered by light itself.” What does light say when we let it speak? It answers in its own vocabulary, a multitude of traces, stains, and silhouettes laid down on photosensitive paper. Unsuspected manifestations of the world, instantaneous and tangible, take shape from the point of view of objects, which watch us in return. To see… and to be seen.

blocks.text: The T3 Photo Festival Tokyo is on view in the Japanese capital city through October 26, 2026, in the Yaesu, Nihonbashi, Kyobashi, and Ginza districts. Free admission.
